Background: The rapid growth of inverter-based resources (IBRs) in the U.S. electric grid has created an urgent need to understand how large renewable facilities can supply essential reliability services traditionally provided by synchronous machines. While significant progress has been made in grid-forming (GFM) controls, weak-grid stability, and EMT modeling, most publicly available studies focus on individual devices, microgrids, or standalone BESS installations. Prior research provides limited insight into coordinated GFM-GFL behavior at the transmission scale. This project evaluates GFM-enabled reliability services in a multi-hundred-megawatt commercial hybrid facility, addressing a critical gap in existing work. 5.1 Current State of the Art in Grid-Forming Inverters and Hybrid IBR Plants Recent work by national laboratories, universities, and OEMs has established the foundation of modern GFM controls, including droop-based methods, virtual synchronous machine (VSM) control, and advanced current-limiting strategies. These studies show that GFM inverters can provide voltage stiffness, frequency support, and improved disturbance recovery, especially under weak-grid conditions. However, most demonstrations have been conducted using single IBR devices or simplified systems. Although prior research has examined weak-grid challenges such as PLL-driven instabilities, multi-IBR oscillations, and sensitivity to short-circuit strength, scaling these findings to large hybrid plants remains largely unaddressed. Public information on GFM wind turbine behavior is particularly limited, and no published studies have evaluated combined GFM wind, GFM BESS, GFL wind, and solar within an integrated utility-scale facility. 5.2 How This Project Addresses the Gaps in Prior Work This project directly addresses these gaps by evaluating GFM behavior within a 380- MW hybrid facility that combines GFM wind, GFM battery storage, GFL wind, and solar, an operating configuration not documented in prior research. The project provides the first integrated assessment of mixed GFM/GFL resource dynamics using detailed EMT models, plant-level control interactions, and system-level validation workflows appropriate for transmission-connected operation. The work also incorporates engineering practices not typically included in academic or pilot-scale studies. These include development of utility-grade GFM performance metrics, multi-stage EMT validation, evaluation of weak-grid and phase-angle disturbances, execution of a 30-mode Failure Modes and Effects Analysis (FMEA), and preparation for commissioning under real interconnection constraints. Additionally, both EMT and positive-sequence GFM models were developed to support planning-level studies and ensure consistency across modeling platforms. Page 6 of 36 Award Number: DE-EE0010651 Recipient Name: Portland General Electric The project leverages insights from DOE-funded national laboratory research, relevant IEEE standards, and existing GFM studies to guide metric development and simulation methodology. It extends these frameworks into a multi-technology, utility- scale context for which no validated public data previously existed. Collectively, the work establishes a reproducible, utility-ready foundation for future hybrid-plant GFM demonstrations. 6.
